title: Reading the notebook through
hookLine: twelve books, never meant to be read by anyone else, now read in order

cards: Someone's private journal, found in a drawer. Not a memoir written for readers. The real thing: notes to self, repeated reminders, the same struggle written down again three months later because it hadn't gone away.
The writer was the emperor of Rome, and notes in the text place parts of it in army camps, at war. Marcus Aurelius has turned up many times on this path, a line here, a passage there.
Starting today, for about four months, no more dipping in.

teach.b: First, the writer. Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome.

As book one shows, Stoic philosophers taught him from his youth, and for years he jotted down notes to himself, in Greek, the language of philosophy for educated Romans, not his native Latin. Second, the title.
The book is known as the Meditations, but as far as anyone knows, he didn't call it that.

The Greek manuscripts carry a heading that means something like to himself, and scholars think a later copyist may have added it. Either way, it's honest: these are things a man said to himself. Third, the shape.

Twelve books of uneven length, made of short entries, some a single line, some a page. The section numbers are later editors' work, and editions sometimes divide them differently. It doesn't read like an argument.
It reads like someone coming back, again and again, to the same few things he needs to remember.
Fourth, it nearly vanished. Historians of the text say that for centuries it is barely mentioned, and that the first printed edition was made from a manuscript that's since been lost.
One more house fire, one more careless librarian, and it might be gone.
So here's the plan: twelve books, in order, about ten days each, with a few days at the end to close the notebook. Book one is different from all the rest.
It's a list of debts: what Marcus learned from each person in his life, one by one, starting with his grandfather.

how: Some readers of the Meditations read it slowly, an entry or two a day, and some keep their own notebook of reminders alongside it.

games.q: reading the notebook through — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus wrote the Meditations in Latin
he wrote in Greek, the language of philosophy for educated Romans.
the manuscripts carry a heading like 'to himself', possibly added later.
the first printed edition was made from a manuscript now lost
one more loss, and we might not have the book at all.

games.q: you're a reader with four months and Marcus's twelve books. how does this path read them?
o: start with book twelve and work back.
games.why: in order, about ten days a book, starting with book one: a list of debts to the people who shaped him.

practice: If you have a copy of the Meditations, open it to book one and just look at the first page; if not, picture a tired man by a lamp, a tent, a pen.
Then turn it around: if you kept a notebook only for yourself, what's the one thing you'd need to write down most often? Let it come.
